items.title: Flip Phillips interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996
items.q: Ralph Burns was the piano player, and I went with Russ Morgan and Ralph went with Charlie Barnet and then he went with Woody, and Ralph told Woody about me.

ctx.x: Great. How did the first time with Woody Herman come about?

The first time with Woody Herman. I was with Russ Morgan before that. No I was with Red Norvo. And Ralph Burns was the piano player, and I went with Russ Morgan and Ralph went with Charlie Barnet and then he went with Woody, and Ralph told Woody about me. You know and I didn’t want to leave Russ Morgan. It was a nice job and all that. But he said he’d write the book around me and all that. And I says okay, so I went with Woody.
Were you “Flip” then? Did you get that nickname before?

items.title: 52150_Charlie Barnet oral history interview
items.q: The interviewer mentions Flip Phillips in the context of other musicians (Frankie Newton, Roy Eldridge) and bandleaders, but the interviewee (Charlie Barnet) does not mention Flip Phillips or indicate a personal or professional connection.

ctx.x: Leonard Feather, in, "The Book of Jazz," devotes some space to white bandleaders who hired black musicians, and there were so very, very few of them in the '30s and early '40s, and of course he gives you credit for having a mixed band, and he mentions the very few others, Artie Shaw having Billie Holiday in the band and Benny Goodman

having Teddy Wilson and Lionel Hampton, and Flip Phillips working with Frankie Newton. Let's see -- at Kelly Stables. But -- and Roy Eldridge, long association with Gene Krupa's big band. But this was something pretty rare during that period. Is that right? I mean --
Oh, yeah, it was rare all right. Although it actually -- I didn't do it to be revolutionary. It just -- it occurred to me as a wonderful idea. I said, "Why hasn't somebody done this?"
